title: The Effect of Network Adoption Subsidies: Evidence from Digital Traces in Rwanda
summary: This study evaluates a 2008 Rwandan government program that subsidized mobile phone handsets in rural areas by analyzing 5.3 billion transaction records. The authors find that while some handsets were resold, the program successfully increased adoption and generated significant welfare benefits, particularly through network spillovers to nonrecipients. The paper also uses a structural model to compare the actual program against alternative targeting strategies, such as voucher-based systems.

title: Behavior Revealed in Mobile Phone Usage Predicts Credit Repayment
summary: This article develops and evaluates a machine learning method to predict credit repayment using mobile phone metadata, specifically for individuals in developing countries who lack traditional financial histories. The authors demonstrate that behavioral patterns extracted from phone usage can outperform traditional credit bureau models in predicting default, offering a viable path for extending credit to the unbanked.

title: Instant Loans Can Lift Subjective Well-Being: A Randomized Evaluation of Digital Credit in Nigeria
summary: This paper presents the results of a randomized controlled trial evaluating the welfare impacts of digital credit in Nigeria. The study finds that auto-approval for digital loans significantly increases subjective well-being, primarily by reducing symptoms of depression, while having no significant impact on other welfare measures like income, expenditures, or resilience.

summary: This paper demonstrates that behavioral patterns extracted from mobile phone metadata can effectively predict credit repayment, particularly for unbanked individuals lacking traditional financial histories. The authors develop a machine learning approach that outperforms traditional credit bureau models in this context and remains stable over time when using within-week variation techniques.

title: The Potential of Digital Credit to Bank the Poor
summary: This article examines how digital credit, enabled by mobile phone usage data, can provide financial services to unbanked populations in developing countries. The authors analyze the predictive power of behavioral data from mobile phone usage to generate credit scores and assess the feasibility of expanding credit to previously excluded groups.

title: The Adoption of Network Goods: Evidence from the Spread of Mobile Phones in Rwanda
summary: This paper develops a structural model to estimate the demand for mobile phones and simulate the adoption of network goods using transaction data from Rwanda. It evaluates the welfare impacts of government policies, specifically rural coverage obligations and telecom taxation, finding that standard metrics often underestimate the welfare costs of taxes in growing networks.

title: Competition in Network Industries: Evidence from the Rwandan Mobile Phone Network
summary: This paper analyzes the impact of competition policy on welfare and investment in the Rwandan mobile phone network using structural estimation and transaction data. The author finds that introducing a competitor could have significantly lowered prices and increased incentives for rural infrastructure investment, resulting in substantial welfare gains. The study highlights the complex trade-offs between business-stealing effects and network externalities in emerging market telecommunications.
